question:
A central question in neurobiology is how the transient programs that pattern neural progenitors are translated into the enormous, stable diversity of neuronal types. Spatial and temporal cues act only briefly, yet each neuron's identity is defined and maintained for life by terminal selector transcription factors (TFs). How a neuron's developmental origin is read out into a particular selector code remains poorly understood. Some current models propose that spatial and temporal origins are inherited independently through separate selectors.

Three candidate results follow. Exactly one is what this study reported.
- Result A: We demonstrate that, in the Drosophila optic lobe, different selectors remain tied to individual patterning axes through physically distinct enhancers, partitioning inputs within the same lineage. Visual system homeobox (Vsx1) spatially patterns a central neuroepithelial domain and later acts as a terminal selector in dozens of neuronal types, most originating exclusively from that domain. Indeed, in Dm2 neurons that originate exclusively from that domain, it remains regulated by neuroepithelial Vsx1 through its domain-specific enhancer, while the neuroblast temporal TF BarH1 activates a distinct terminal selector through an enhancer of its own. Combining in vivo reporters with sequence-to-accessibility deep-learning models, we identify and disrupt the key binding sites in this BarH1-dependent enhancer, impairing its Dm2-specific activity. Reciprocally, the temporal TF Homeobrain (Hbn) acts as a terminal selector in the related neuron Mi21 within its neuroblast temporal window: its expression in these late-born neurons is not placed under dorsoventral spatial control. Patterning inputs therefore remain partitioned across separate selectors, preserving the independent readout of spatial and temporal origins and revealing a cis-regulatory logic that re-encodes this limited set of inputs into vast neuronal diversity without convergence between axes.
- Result B: We show instead that, in the Drosophila optic lobe, the same selector can be activated by different patterning axes through physically distinct enhancers, even within the same lineage. Visual system homeobox (Vsx1) spatially patterns a central neuroepithelial domain and later acts as a terminal selector in dozens of neuronal types, most originating exclusively from that domain. However, in Dm2 neurons that are produced from every domain, it is regulated not by neuroepithelial Vsx1 but by the neuroblast temporal TF BarH1, through an enhancer distinct from its domain-specific ones. Combining in vivo reporters with sequence-to-accessibility deep-learning models, we identify and disrupt the key binding sites in this enhancer, impairing its Dm2-specific activity. Reciprocally, the temporal TF Homeobrain (Hbn) acts as a terminal selector in the related neuron Mi21 independently of its neuroblast temporal window: its expression in these late-born neurons is instead placed under dorsoventral spatial control. Patterning inputs therefore need not be partitioned across separate selectors but converge combinatorially on the modular enhancers of shared ones, revealing a cis-regulatory logic that re-encodes this limited set of inputs into vast neuronal diversity.
- Result C: We show instead that, in the Drosophila optic lobe, the same selector can be activated by different patterning axes through a single shared enhancer, even within the same lineage. Visual system homeobox (Vsx1) spatially patterns a central neuroepithelial domain and later acts as a terminal selector in dozens of neuronal types, most originating exclusively from that domain. However, in Dm2 neurons that are produced from every domain, it is regulated not by neuroepithelial Vsx1 but by the neuroblast temporal TF BarH1, through an enhancer shared with its domain-specific inputs. Combining in vivo reporters with sequence-to-accessibility deep-learning models, we identify and disrupt the key binding sites in this enhancer, impairing its Dm2-specific activity. Reciprocally, the temporal TF Homeobrain (Hbn) acts as a terminal selector in the related neuron Mi21 independently of its neuroblast temporal window: its expression in these late-born neurons is instead placed under dorsoventral spatial control through a shared enhancer as well. Patterning inputs therefore need not be partitioned across separate selectors but converge combinatorially on shared enhancers, revealing a cis-regulatory logic that re-encodes this limited set of inputs into vast neuronal diversity.
Which result did this study report? Rank the candidates, and give the mechanism, the key evidence, and a validation experiment for the top pick.
